questions.question: What does `io.Copy` do, and why is it suitable for large streams?
questions.title: Streaming data with io.Copy
questions.direct_answer: `io.Copy(dst, src)` transfers bytes from an `io.Reader` to an `io.Writer` until the source reaches EOF or either side fails. It returns the number written and the first error; normal EOF becomes a nil error. Copy works incrementally, so total memory does not grow with the complete file or response size.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The argument order is destination first, source second.
Copy continues until source EOF or an error.
Normal EOF is reported as a nil error.
The returned count is the number of bytes written.
Copy does not close or flush either endpoint.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`io.Copy` connects a source Reader to a destination Writer and transfers until the source ends or an operation fails. The signature puts the destination first: `io.Copy(dst, src)`. It returns the number of bytes successfully written and the first error encountered.

The operation is incremental rather than a read-all-then-write design, so it can move a multi-gigabyte file or HTTP body with bounded working memory. When the source ends normally with `io.EOF`, Copy consumes that condition and returns a nil error because reaching the defined end is success.

For example, copying from `strings.NewReader("streamed data")` into a `bytes.Buffer` returns 13 and leaves the same text in the buffer. The identical call shape works for two files or a response body and a file without materializing the whole source in one byte slice.

Copy owns only the transfer. It does not close files, close response bodies, flush a buffered destination, make a partial destination atomic, or apply a size limit. The caller still owns those lifecycle and policy decisions and must treat a non-nil error together with the possibly nonzero byte count.

sections.title: Copy connects capabilities without owning them
sections.content:
The Reader produces a sequence of bytes and the Writer consumes it. Copy repeatedly moves available data while preserving the endpoints' own implementations. This keeps transfer code independent of storage and transport types.

A failure can occur after useful progress, so the destination may already contain the reported number of bytes. File replacement or protocol code must decide whether that partial output can remain, be removed, or be resumed.

sections.title: EOF is completion, not a transfer error
sections.content:
At the Reader level EOF is the signal that no further input exists. Since Copy's purpose is to continue through that exact point, it translates ordinary EOF into `err == nil`. Other read errors and write errors stop the operation and are returned.

The implementation can use ordinary buffered copying or specialised interfaces exposed by an endpoint. That optimisation does not change the public count-and-error contract, so application code should not depend on an assumed buffer size or number of calls.

sections.title: Copy's responsibility boundary
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[src io.Reader] -->|chunks or fast path| B[io.Copy]
  B --> C[dst io.Writer]
  C --> D[count, first error]
  E[caller] -. owns Close / Flush / limits .-> A
  E -. owns partial-output policy .-> C
```

questions.question: How does `io.Copy` use `WriterTo` and `ReaderFrom` fast paths?
questions.title: io.Copy fast-path interfaces
questions.direct_answer: Before allocating a normal transfer buffer, `io.Copy` checks whether the source implements `io.WriterTo` and calls `src.WriteTo(dst)`. If not, it checks whether the destination implements `io.ReaderFrom` and calls `dst.ReadFrom(src)`. These optional interfaces let an endpoint use a more efficient transfer while preserving Copy's byte-count and error contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The source's `WriterTo` fast path is checked first.
The destination's `ReaderFrom` path is checked second.
Only when neither applies does Copy use its ordinary loop.
Fast paths preserve the same written-count and error result.
`CopyBuffer` also ignores its supplied buffer when a fast path applies.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`io.Copy` is interface-aware. It first asks whether the source implements `io.WriterTo`. If so, the source performs the transfer by calling `WriteTo(dst)`. Otherwise Copy asks whether the destination implements `io.ReaderFrom` and lets the destination pull through `ReadFrom(src)`.

These paths allow a concrete endpoint to use knowledge that a generic loop lacks. A file or buffer may transfer directly, reuse internal storage, or choose a specialised system operation. The optimisation remains hidden behind the same `(written, error)` contract.

For example, a custom source can implement both Reader and WriterTo. Calling `io.Copy` marks its WriterTo method as used and writes the payload without invoking its fallback Read. If the destination also has ReaderFrom, the source still wins because WriterTo is checked first.

This matters when wrapping endpoints. A wrapper that exposes only Read can hide the underlying WriterTo method and change performance, even though correctness remains. It also means a buffer passed to `io.CopyBuffer` may never be touched. I optimise only after measuring and keep wrapper behaviour explicit.

sections.title: Optional capabilities refine a minimal interface
sections.content:
Reader and Writer are sufficient for correctness. WriterTo and ReaderFrom add transfer capability without forcing every implementation to provide it. Copy performs dynamic interface checks and selects the most specialised available path.

The order prevents competing endpoints from both controlling the operation: source WriterTo has priority, then destination ReaderFrom, then the generic loop. Tests can observe this order with small instrumented types.

sections.title: Wrappers can preserve or hide performance capabilities
sections.content:
Embedding an interface value and exposing only its Read method can intentionally suppress WriterTo. Conversely, a transparent wrapper may forward WriterTo so the optimisation survives. Both are legal, but middleware authors should understand the performance consequence.

Fast paths are implementation details from the application's perspective. The caller must still check the returned count and error and manage endpoint cleanup. A specialised transfer cannot turn an incomplete copy into success.

sections.title: Copy fast-path selection order
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[io.Copy dst, src] --> B{src implements WriterTo?}
  B -- Yes --> C[src.WriteTo dst]
  B -- No --> D{dst implements ReaderFrom?}
  D -- Yes --> E[dst.ReadFrom src]
  D -- No --> F[generic buffered loop]
  C --> G[written, error]
  E --> G
  F --> G
```

questions.question: When should you use `io.CopyN` or `io.CopyBuffer` instead of `io.Copy`?
questions.title: CopyN and CopyBuffer boundaries
questions.direct_answer: Use `io.CopyN` when exactly a maximum of N bytes belong to the operation and an early source end must be reported. Use `io.CopyBuffer` when the generic copy loop should reuse a caller-owned non-empty buffer. Keep `io.Copy` for an unrestricted transfer when custom buffer ownership offers no measured benefit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `CopyN` succeeds only when exactly N bytes are written.
An early EOF from CopyN is returned as an error.
`CopyBuffer` reuses a supplied staging slice in the generic path.
A nil buffer is allocated; a non-nil zero-length buffer panics.
WriterTo or ReaderFrom fast paths can bypass the supplied buffer.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`io.CopyN(dst, src, n)` places a byte boundary on the transfer. It returns success exactly when the written count equals n. If the source ends first, the count shows the partial progress and the error tells the caller that the fixed-length record was incomplete.

`io.CopyBuffer` has the same completion behaviour as Copy but accepts staging storage supplied by the caller. It is useful when a controlled loop reuses buffers to reduce allocations. Nil asks the function to allocate normally, while a non-nil slice with zero length causes a panic.

For example, CopyN can take the four-byte prefix `"HEAD"` from a longer stream. A separate CopyBuffer call can transfer `"payload"` through a three-byte reusable slice when both endpoints expose only their basic Reader and Writer methods.

Fast paths still apply: source WriterTo or destination ReaderFrom can make the CopyBuffer slice irrelevant. A small buffer can also increase calls rather than improve throughput. I use CopyN for protocol or safety boundaries and CopyBuffer only when profiling or ownership design justifies explicit reuse.

sections.title: One variant limits bytes; the other controls staging memory
sections.content:
CopyN changes the logical contract by requiring a fixed number of bytes. CopyBuffer leaves the logical range unchanged and only changes where temporary storage comes from when the generic loop is selected.

These decisions should not be conflated. A caller can need a byte limit without a custom buffer, or buffer reuse without a transfer limit. The APIs keep those concerns separate.

sections.title: Bounds belong at the protocol edge
sections.content:
A fixed-length field, upload quota, or prefix extraction can use CopyN directly or combine `io.LimitReader` with other processing. The caller must still decide whether bytes after the limit are another record, forbidden input, or deliberately ignored.

For CopyBuffer, the slice must remain owned by the call until it returns. Reusing one buffer concurrently across transfers is unsafe because both calls can mutate it. Buffer pools need a strict acquire-use-release lifecycle.

sections.title: Choose the copy contract
sections.content:
| Function | Transfer boundary | Staging memory | Early EOF |
|---|---|---|---|
| `io.Copy` | Until source EOF | Internal or fast path | Normal success |
| `io.CopyN` | Exactly N bytes | Internal / destination fast path | Error before N |
| `io.CopyBuffer` | Until source EOF | Caller slice or fast path | Normal success |

sections.title: Use a fixed prefix and a caller-owned copy buffer
